relationship: Seven-year release and later public-reading appointment
rationale: The seven-year release is named again in Moses' appointment of public law reading at the Feast of the Pitching of Tents in the release year.

relationship: Seventh-year release and later communal undertaking
rationale: The instruction to make a release after seven years corresponds to the community's undertaking to release the seventh year and the demand of every hand.

relationship: Debt-release instruction and later release undertaking
rationale: The command to release a neighbour's debt and refrain from exacting it corresponds to Nehemiah's undertaking to release the demand of every hand in the seventh year.

relationship: Same-chapter debt-release scope and explicit distinction
rationale: The requirement to release a brother's debt repeats the preceding rule, while this verse distinguishes the foreigner from whom the debt may still be exacted.

relationship: Same-chapter promised absence of need and its condition
rationale: The promised absence of need through the Lord's blessing in the inherited land is followed by the explicit condition of diligently hearing and keeping His commandments.

relationship: Same-chapter command-keeping condition and preceding promise
rationale: Diligent obedience states the condition attached to the preceding assurance of blessing and absence of need, rather than presenting that assurance without its stated qualification.

relationship: Repeated lending and rule blessing
rationale: Both promise lending to many nations without borrowing and ruling without being ruled; chapter28 places the assurance within blessings explicitly conditioned on command keeping.

relationship: Support rather than financial exploitation of a poor brother
rationale: Both address an impoverished brother and require supporting him; Deuteronomy prohibits closing the hand, while Leviticus specifically prohibits interest or increase on money and food.

relationship: Same-chapter open-hand response to the stated need
rationale: The command to open the hands and lend according to need answers the preceding prohibition on withholding affection and closing the hand against a needy brother.

relationship: Same-chapter release rule and warning against evading its effect
rationale: The approaching release year must not become a reason to withhold help; the opening rule explains the anticipated debt release behind that particular temptation.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated sufficient lending with willing giving
rationale: Both require open-handed provision and lending sufficient for the brother's need; verse10 additionally prohibits a grieving heart and promises blessing upon the giver's work.

relationship: Continuing presence of the poor and opportunity to help
rationale: The statement that the needy will not cease grounds an open-hand command; Jesus likewise says the poor remain with the hearers and they can do them good.

relationship: Same-chapter need statements with their distinct qualifications
rationale: The continuing-needy statement grounds the duty to help, while the earlier absence-of-need promise is joined to divine blessing and diligent obedience; neither statement is silently removed.

relationship: Six-year Hebrew service and seventh-year freedom
rationale: Both require freedom in the seventh year after six years of Hebrew service; Deuteronomy expressly includes a Hebrew woman in this instruction.

relationship: Same-chapter prohibition of empty release and specified provision
rationale: The instruction not to release the servant empty is developed by generous provision from sheep, grain and winepress according to the owner's received blessing.

relationship: Same-chapter departure gifts implement nonempty release
rationale: The specified sheep, grain and winepress provision implements the preceding prohibition against sending the freed servant away empty, with divine blessing setting the measure.

relationship: Egyptian redemption as reason for service obligations
rationale: Both ground obligations concerning Israelite servants in the Lord's redemption from Egypt; Leviticus describes them as His servants and restricts their sale, while Deuteronomy commands remembered bondage.

relationship: Servant's stated love and refusal of release
rationale: Both describe a servant declaring love and refusing freedom; Deuteronomy names the master and household's wellbeing, while Exodus expressly names master, wife and children.

relationship: Awl, ear and doorway procedure for lasting service
rationale: Both prescribe piercing the ear with an awl at a doorway and lasting service; Exodus adds the tribunal and doorpost, while Deuteronomy explicitly extends the instruction to a female servant.

relationship: Six-year service and required release
rationale: The owner must not resent releasing someone who served six years, corresponding to Exodus' six-year service and seventh-year freedom; Deuteronomy's yearly-wage comparison remains its own wording.

relationship: Firstborn male livestock belonging to the Lord
rationale: Both identify firstborn male cattle and sheep as belonging or sanctified to the Lord; Deuteronomy additionally prohibits work with the firstborn calf and shearing the firstborn sheep.

relationship: Firstborn meal at the chosen place
rationale: The annual household eating before the Lord at His chosen place corresponds to the earlier restriction on firstborn consumption in cities and direction to eat it before Him.

relationship: Blemished animals excluded from sacrifice
rationale: Both reject blemished animals as offerings and explicitly include blindness; Deuteronomy additionally names lameness, while Leviticus supplies its own longer list and offering context.

relationship: Repeated local clean-and-unclean meat permission
rationale: Both permit clean and unclean persons alike to eat locally as gazelle and deer are eaten; the current context concerns the blemished firstborn rather than ordinary meat generally.

relationship: Repeated blood prohibition and earth-water disposal formula
rationale: Both prohibit eating blood and require pouring it onto the earth like water, retaining the same particular restriction alongside their respective local meat permissions.

relationship: Departure month and Unleavened Bread remembrance
rationale: Both connect the prescribed observance with the month of new produce or new grain and departure from Egypt, preserving their respective month descriptions and festival emphasis.

relationship: Nighttime Egyptian deliverance context
rationale: The Passover remembrance expressly recalls departure by night; Exodus narrates the midnight firstborn judgment and Pharaoh summoning Moses and Aaron at night to order Israel's departure.

relationship: Passover sacrifice with differing livestock and setting details
rationale: Both command the Passover sacrifice; Deuteronomy names sheep and cattle at the chosen place, while Exodus instructs Israelite households in Egypt concerning a lamb or young goat and its evening slaughter.

relationship: Unleavened bread and hasty departure
rationale: Deuteronomy calls the bread affliction and recalls departure in haste; Exodus explains the unleavened cakes by the Egyptians driving Israel out before the dough could leaven.

relationship: Seven-day unleavened observance as departure memorial
rationale: Both prescribe seven days of unleavened bread in connection with the departure from Egypt, with Exodus also setting first- and seventh-day assemblies and work restrictions.

relationship: Passover flesh not retained until morning
rationale: Both forbid leaving the sacrificed flesh until morning; Exodus additionally commands burning what remains, while Deuteronomy specifies the evening sacrifice of the first day.

relationship: Seven-day absence of leaven
rationale: Both require leaven to be absent for seven days; Deuteronomy describes all the borders, while Exodus specifies houses and the consequence for eating leavened food.

relationship: Same-chapter prohibited city sacrifice and chosen destination
rationale: The prohibition on sacrificing Passover in any of the cities is immediately answered by the command to sacrifice at the Lord's chosen place at evening.

relationship: Passover slaughter at evening
rationale: Both assign Passover slaughter to evening; Deuteronomy further specifies sunset, the departure remembrance and the chosen place, whereas Exodus supplies the fourteenth-day household arrangement.

relationship: Passover preparation instructions with preserved difference
rationale: Deuteronomy says to boil and roast and eat at the chosen place; Exodus prescribes roasting with fire and explicitly prohibits boiling in water, without harmonizing those instructions.

relationship: Unleavened observance and concluding work restriction
rationale: Deuteronomy specifies six days and a seventh-day concluding feast; Exodus states seven days and first- and seventh-day holiness, with both allowing work for a person's necessary needs.

relationship: Seven-week counting with distinct starting descriptions
rationale: Both require seven complete weeks; Deuteronomy begins with the sickle's first harvest, while Leviticus counts from the day after the Sabbath and sheaf presentation, then names fifty days.

relationship: Feast of Weeks and harvest observance
rationale: Both command keeping the Feast of Weeks; Exodus explicitly names the beginning of wheat harvest, while Deuteronomy measures the observance by ability and received blessing.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated inclusive festival rejoicing
rationale: The Weeks rejoicing and later Tents rejoicing both name the household, slaves, Levite, sojourner, orphan and widow, keeping the two feasts distinct despite the shared participant list.

relationship: Egyptian household bondage remembered in communal obligations
rationale: Both command remembrance of household slavery in Egypt as motivation for the surrounding obligations; chapter15 concerns servant release, while this instruction follows inclusive festival rejoicing.

relationship: Seven-day ingathering feast with distinct additional details
rationale: Both connect a seven-day celebration with gathered produce; Leviticus additionally names the seventh-month date, branches, tent dwelling and the explanatory memory of wilderness tents.

relationship: Same-chapter shared participant list across distinct feasts
rationale: The Tents rejoicing repeats the Weeks list of household, slaves, Levite, sojourner, orphan and widow, preserving the particular inclusive pattern without merging the festivals.

relationship: Seven-day harvest rejoicing before the Lord
rationale: Both specify seven days of harvest celebration and rejoicing before the Lord; Deuteronomy names His chosen place and blessing, whereas Leviticus specifies the calendar and branches.

relationship: Three annual appearances and named agricultural feasts
rationale: Both prescribe three annual appearances for males and name unleavened and harvest-related feasts; Deuteronomy explicitly names Weeks and Tents and the chosen place, preserving differing festival labels.

relationship: Same-chapter nonempty appearance and proportionate gift
rationale: Giving according to ability and divine blessing specifies how the preceding prohibition on appearing empty before the Lord is to be fulfilled.

relationship: Appointment and righteous work of tribal judges
rationale: The command to appoint judges and recording officers by tribes corresponds to Moses' earlier appointment of graded leaders and recording officers, with instructions for just hearings and difficult cases.

relationship: Judgment and gifts that corrupt judicial sight and words
rationale: Both prohibit perverting judgment and receiving corrupting gifts, explaining that such gifts blind the eyes and distort righteous words; Deuteronomy additionally names partiality.

relationship: Pursuit of justice and concrete impartial judgment
rationale: The command to pursue what is just corresponds to Leviticus' requirement of righteous neighbour judgment without favouring poor or powerful, while Deuteronomy adds life and land inheritance.

relationship: Sacred grove forbidden beside the Lord's altar
rationale: The ban on planting a sacred grove beside the Lord's altar corresponds to the instruction to cut down the nations' sacred groves rather than adopt those installations.

relationship: Parallel prohibition on erecting a pillar
rationale: Both prohibit setting up a pillar; Leviticus includes it among forbidden images and worship stones, while Deuteronomy states that the Lord has hated it.
